newsitem.title: CHINA: Japanese begin late attack on China candy market.
newsitem.headline: Japanese begin late attack on China candy market.

text.p: Kanro begins construction on Wednesday of the first joint venture by a Japanese confectionery maker in China, in a belated attack on the booming Chinese market, industry officials said on Monday.

Concerns over unstable investment rules and the cost of importing expensive equipment and raw materials has dissuaded Japanese candymakers from production in China, company officials said at an exhibition of their goods in a Shanghai hotel.

Kanro's factory, in the southeast coastal city of Shantou, is a joint venture 40 percent owned by itself, 30 percent by Mitsubishi Corp and 30 percent by Four Seas Mercantile Holdings of Hong Kong, said Mercantile official Zheng Jialin.
"All output will be sold in China, where the confectionery market is growing about 20 percent a year, with Shanghai alone consuming five million tonnes in 1995," Zheng said.
"The gap in standard between domestic and imported candy is narrowing, but imported brands cost at least double," he said.
To reduce this price gap, foreign companies such as Nestle and Cadbury Schweppes PLC have started to produce in plants in China and sell to the local market.
Foreign brand chocolate bars and candy are on sale at many streetside shops and department stores in Shanghai.
Ryuichi Suzuki, senior managing director of Denroku Co, held up a 140-gramme packet of his company's chocolate beans that sell for 184 yen ($1.6) in Japan and 21.5 yuan ($2.6) in China.
"Our production costs in Japan are very high because we have to pay much higher than world prices for sugar, chocolate and other raw materials," he said.
Japanese makers are considering investment in China, but there are risks including high costs and restrictions on what they can do, he said.

Most Japanese candy makers do not even consider overseas production, said Koji Ukai, president of Ukai Yakkoame Honpo Co Ltd. "The key to such investment is the taste. You cannot just copy the same taste you have at home."
"We need to research what taste suits the Chinese. Western candies are sweeter than those made in Japan," he said.
Another Japanese producer, who declined to be identified, was more blunt about why Japanese candymakers have not invested.
"If this were Malaysia or Thailand we would decide on an investment at once. But this is China. We do not believe in the government -- it may change its policy.
"The government is still communist. Many Japanese do not trust it," he said. "China is very difficult. We are very careful and do not want to invest too much."
Latest official figures put China's 1994 chocolate output at 22,000 tonnes, up from 9,500 in 1988. There were no later figures immediately available.
An Nestle official in Shanghai said the company was already producing peppermint and smarties in China and planned to produce chocolate.
"Market competition is very fierce between local brands, those made in joint venture plants and imports," she said.
"Japanese candies are very well packaged but are too expensive. The strongest local brand is Big White Rabbit, which does well on price and brand loyalty," she added.
